problem: Deep RL solutions to partially observable visual labyrinth navigation (ViZDoom My Way Home) need convolutional embeddings and recurrent memory, and are hard to decompose or deploy on small platforms. Prior TPG solutions for ViZDoom were large, indexed over half the pixels, or were trained on multiple tasks at once.
motivation: Braitenberg vehicles show that complex behaviour can emerge from simple reactive heuristics, but this becomes hard with high-dimensional pixel state. The authors hypothesise that a heavily constrained genetic programming representation (arithmetic instructions only, direct pixel indexing, no convolution or memory) will bias evolution toward simple, interpretable reactive navigation heuristics.
key_idea: Evolve small Tangled Program Graphs, which index only a tiny fraction of pixels and have no memory, so that Braitenberg-style wall-following and re-orientation heuristics emerge to solve the My Way Home labyrinth.
insight: Sparse pixel indexing with an arithmetic-only instruction set biases evolution toward simple reactive heuristics. In the empty-room no-goal experiment, the TPG champion shows a slow clockwise arc, wall alignment and alternating arc direction, whereas DQN only meanders and follows the wall. Its labyrinth success comes from exploiting the maze geometry (corridor following, using room sides to re-orient) rather than from seeing the goal. DQN succeeds only from the two rooms nearest the goal, where the vest is visible.
method: Linear GP programs: instructions <mode,target,op,source/input> over 8 registers, using arithmetic ops {+,-,÷,×} and direct pixel indexing of the 160x120 frame, max 128 instructions
Learner: a context program (bids via R[0]) plus either an action program (register vector, argmax gives the action) or a pointer to another ensemble
Ensemble: 2-4 learners; the highest context bid wins and its action program runs, or decision-making is deferred to the pointed ensemble, forming a graph
Breeder evolution: population 120, worst 50% deleted, clone+crossover+mutate ensembles and learners; fitness is the average episodic reward over 5 spawns
Two-phase training: P1 (500 gens) P_action=0 gives single-node teams; P2 (500 gens) P_action=0.5 lets action programs become ensemble pointers, building graphs
DQN baseline: the ViZDoom PyTorch example DQN with 5-frame stacking and no recurrent memory, used to show task difficulty
Behavioural analysis: spawn-path plots per room and an empty single-room no-goal test (also with per-room textures) to expose the heuristic

setting.backbone: Tangled Program Graphs (linear GP, evolved from scratch); DQN baseline (CNN, trained from scratch)
setting.model_size: Champions average 3.4±2.8 ensembles and 13.6±11.2 learners; programs index about 27-36 pixels (≤0.8% of state per decision)
setting.training_data: Trained online in ViZDoom My Way Home with uniform random spawn points and random orientation; 5 independent TPG runs; no extra data
setting.observation: Monocular first-person RGB/pixel frame 160x120 (19,200 pixels), partially observable, no memory
setting.action_space: 3 discrete actions: move forward, turn left, turn right

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 spawns with random orientation in each of the 17 rooms/corridors
numbers.extra: Cumulative reward, not SR; max 1.0, failure gives -0.21 (2100 steps × -0.0001)
numbers.evidence: Table 2: Test performance on MWH task scenario; TPG 0.561 / 0.867 / 0.997 / -0.21

numbers_note: Only cumulative reward is reported (no SR, SPL or NE). Per-room results are given only as violin plots.
results: The TPG champion reaches an average test reward of 0.561 (median 0.867), against -0.094 (median -0.21) for the memoryless DQN, which only succeeds from the rooms nearest the goal. TPG champions use ≤0.8% of the pixels per decision and show consistent wall-following and re-orientation behaviour.
limitations: Evaluation is a single labyrinth with a fixed goal and symmetric, centred room/corridor layout, so it is unclear whether the heuristics generalize to other layouts
Only a weak memoryless DQN baseline was compared (no recurrent or intrinsic-motivation methods) and performance is only reward-based, with poor results in rooms 24 and 25
Behavioural analysis is qualitative and based on a single champion; the heuristic does not fully account for exits from corridors or corners
